tagline.text: A Wall of Remembrance and museum in Quezon City honoring those who stood against martial law

location.label: Location
location.text: Quezon Avenue near the EDSA intersection, Barangay Pinyahan, Diliman, Quezon City (Bantayog Center, Salonga Building)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (indoor visit, so possible year-round)

children.text: A memorial in Quezon City to those who died or fought against the Marcos regime (1972–1986). In one place you can see the roughly 14-meter Inang Bayan statue, the Wall of Remembrance with engraved names, a museum and an archive.

Bantayog ng mga Bayani means "Monument to the Heroes" in Tagalog. It stands near where Quezon Avenue meets EDSA in Diliman, Quezon City, in Barangay Pinyahan. After the 1986 People Power Revolution, a Filipino-American physician, Dr. Ruben Mallari, proposed a memorial to those who resisted during martial law, and a group of like-minded people formed a foundation. According to the foundation, the monument and the Wall of Remembrance were unveiled on
November 30, 1992
, while the Quezon City government's page says the center opened in 2007.
There are two centerpieces. One is the "Inang Bayan" (Mother Philippines) statue by sculptor Eduardo Castrillo, about

(35 feet) tall, showing a woman reaching toward the sky while holding a fallen young man. The other is the Wall of Remembrance behind it, black granite slabs engraved with the names of people who died fighting the regime during martial law or devoted themselves to resistance. The first 65 were enshrined in 1992, from 1993 heroes who died after the EDSA Revolution were also included, and 332 names were on the wall as of the
November 30
, 2023 ceremony. Names are added each year after review. The grounds were designed by National Artist Ildefonso Santos Jr.

Behind the wall is a building named after Senator Jovito Salonga. The ground floor has a library and archive, and the second floor has the museum (Museo ng Bantayog), a memorial hall introducing the people on the wall by profession, and the small Yuchengco Auditorium. The museum covers more than 100 square meters, and the foundation says about 100,000 people have visited since it opened. Photos, documents and objects take you from the atmosphere before martial law was declared to People Power in 1986, and a replica of a political prisoner's cell stands out.

This is closer to a place for learning history than a tourist attraction. It is recommended for anyone who wants to understand modern Philippine history, especially the martial law era under Marcos, or who would like to talk about history with Filipino friends. The regime lasted a long time, so time passes quickly as you read the exhibit panels. If you want a guide, contact the center beforehand and ask. Combined with Quezon Memorial Circle, it makes a one-day outing that covers the flow of modern Philippine history. Quiet, respectful behavior is the basic rule. Real people's names are engraved on the wall, so do not climb on it or pose playfully when taking photos. Photography rules may vary over time, so ask the staff at the entrance. First-time visitors are advised to start at the Wall of Remembrance and then go up to the museum. If you look at the names first, read the flow of the era in the museum, and then return to the wall at the end, the same names read very differently. If you have visited a memorial to a democracy movement in Korea, you will find the context easy to relate to, and going with a Filipino friend or local guide gives you much to talk about. The site is not large, so plan it as a calm time for reading and reflecting rather than big expectations.
A bronze statue about

tall by sculptor Eduardo Castrillo. Mother Philippines reaches toward the sky while holding a fallen young man, symbolizing those who fell for the country. It is a striking sight that can also be seen from the Quezon Avenue side.

Each black granite slab is engraved with the names of those who stood against the regime during martial law. As of November 2023, 332 names were on the wall, and a ceremony adding new names is held around
November 30
each year. It is a semicircular outdoor space where you can sit and read slowly.

On the second floor of the Salonga Building, it shows the history of the Marcos regime and the resistance through photographs, documents and objects. It follows the flow from the situation before martial law and the repression during the regime to the 1986 People Power Revolution, and special exhibits change from time to time.

This space introduces the faces and stories of people whose names are on the Wall of Remembrance, grouped by occupation such as students, workers and religious members. Once you know what kind of lives the names belonged to, the wall feels different.

The museum is described as having a corner that recreates a cell where political prisoners were held. Seeing the cramped space in person conveys the atmosphere of the era better than reading about it. Displays may be reorganized, so check when you visit.

The ground floor has a library and archive of newspapers, magazines, books and documents from the martial law period, used by students, journalists and researchers. A traveler will not stay long, but it is valuable material for anyone studying modern Philippine history in depth.
A small auditorium named after Ambassador Alfonso Yuchengco, used for film screenings and foundation events. If you go as a group, it is worth asking in advance whether a screening can be arranged.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: From the Wall of Remembrance to the museum and a nearby walk

children.text: Arrive soon after opening, pay admission (
according to the Quezon City page), and sign the visitor record. For groups or a guide, it is safer to contact the center in advance.
Start outdoors with the Inang Bayan statue and the Wall of Remembrance, taking your time. If you note a few names, you will meet them again in the museum.
Take a quick look at the ground-floor library and archive, then go up to the second-floor museum by stairs or lift.
Follow the museum exhibits in chronological order. Allow about
1 hour
for the timeline before and after martial law, the photographs and the cell replica corner.
Read about the lives of people introduced by occupation in the memorial hall. Finally, come back down to the Wall of Remembrance for one more look.
Have lunch near Eton Centris. There is no confirmed information about a restaurant inside the center, so eat outside.
If you have time, continue to Quezon Memorial Circle for a walk.

Opening hours differ between sources (one record lists separate morning and afternoon sessions on weekdays), so rather than planning a separate afternoon slot, finishing everything in the morning is safer. Weekend and holiday operation is not certain, so contact the center first.

items.title: Full-day history trip
items.subtitle: Surveying modern Philippine history in Quezon City

children.text: Begin at the Bantayog Center to hear the story of the martial law era first.
Have lunch at Eton Centris or a nearby food area.
Move to Quezon Memorial Circle and look around the Manuel Quezon monument and the park.
As the sun lowers, stroll the park paths and head back. To avoid rush-hour traffic, it is better to leave early.

From central Manila (Malate, Ermita), you can take the MRT-3 toward Quezon Avenue station or ride a Grab taxi. Check locally the walking distance and route between Quezon Avenue station and the center.
By bus, one described route is to take a UE Letre bus on EDSA, get off in front of Eton Centris, and walk behind the mall (based on a 2019 article, so routes may have changed).
EDSA and Quezon Avenue are very congested at rush hour. If possible, go after 10:00 or on a weekday midday.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport, a Grab or taxi is the simplest option. Travel time varies greatly with traffic and can take more than 1 hour.
With a lot of luggage, it is easier to drop it at your hotel first and visit light.
The center has only two areas, the outdoor plaza and the Salonga Building, so you can see it all on foot.
You can reach Quezon Memorial Circle by Grab or jeepney, but ask locally for the exact jeepney route.

The visit works year-round because the exhibits are indoors and the plaza is outdoors, but the Wall of Remembrance is outside and affected by weather. The dry season, December to May, is the best for walking.
Around
November 30
each year a ceremony is held to add new names to the Wall of Remembrance. On that day it gets crowded and general visits may be restricted, so it is best to check the latest announcements.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: A good time to photograph the outdoor wall and the statue.
Visit in the morning and cool down inside the museum.
Bring an umbrella. A commemorative ceremony is held around November 30.

Around the center there are malls including Eton Centris, which make meals and light shopping easy. The choices are wide, from Korean restaurants to Filipino home cooking and fast food, so it is a good place to spend time before or after your visit.
There are many hotels along EDSA and across Quezon City. Many people also come for a day trip from central Manila (Malate, Makati).

For a meal near the center, a mall is the simplest choice. Lunch is quieter on weekdays around noon than on weekends, and in the heat of the day a cafe inside a mall is a good place to rest before the afternoon. If you try local street food, check the hygiene yourself and bring bottled water.
Before going, call (8298-2298 according to the Quezon City page) or email the foundation to confirm it is open. Hours differ between sources, so it is easy to make a wasted trip.
Exhibit explanations may be in English and Filipino, so prepare a translation app and, if possible, ask for a guide.
Marcos and martial law are still sensitive topics in Philippine society. Be careful when asking locals for their opinions.
Stay quiet at the Wall of Remembrance and do not lean on it or climb on it.
Viewing may be restricted during the November 30 ceremony, so avoid that date or check announcements.
Bring small cash. It is safer to check locally how admission can be paid.
This is different from Libingan ng mga Bayani, the heroes' cemetery in Taguig. The names are similar, so avoid mixing them up on map apps.

Opening hours and admission differ between sources, so be sure to confirm by phone or email before you go. A center with the same name also exists in Bulacan, so check on the map that you have the Quezon City one.
Traffic around Quezon Avenue and EDSA is heavy, so allow plenty of travel time.
Watch for pickpockets and phone snatchers, and leave valuables at your hotel.
Do not argue loudly about politically sensitive topics.
On days with events or school groups, it may be crowded and some areas may be closed.
Holiday opening has not been confirmed, so check the latest announcements.
A large park with a tower honoring President Manuel Quezon. It is about
10–20 minutes
by car, depending on traffic.
A mall right near the center, convenient for meals and rest. It is also described as the bus drop-off point.
A street lined with restaurants and shops where you can glimpse everyday Filipino life.
